extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning how to write and read proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing and assessing mathematical proofs: defines what a proof is, the dual goals of proof writing, precise logical vocabulary, and a practical table of proof techniques (how to prove, how to use, how to negate common statement types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: "A mathematical proof is an argument which convinces other people that something is true."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Math aims to prove things beyond any doubt in principle. Caveats: people make mistakes and total rigor can be impractical for very large projects; there are foundational subtleties (e.g., Gödel). A proof's primary purpose is to convince; it should be an argument that other mathematicians accept as establishing truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two roles of a good proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof should (1) convince other mathematicians the statement is true and (2) help them understand why it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective proofs achieve both persuasion and explanation; writing should serve both purposes rather than only asserting truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise logical vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logical words with their mathematical meanings (not, and, or, if...then, iff, ∀, ∃).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific notes: 'or' is inclusive in mathematics (never 'exclusive or'); 'if...then' (p ⇒ q) is false only when p is true and q is false and is vacuously true when p is false; 'iff' means equivalence; order of quantifiers matters (∀x∃y x<y true, ∃y∀x x<y false); definitions often use 'if' to mean 'iff' (a conventional abuse). Being precise about these meanings is essential to correct proofs and correct reading of statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify statement type and use the matching proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the target statement is a simple assertion, a conjunction, a disjunction, an implication, a biconditional, an existential, or a universal statement, then apply the appropriate proof technique from the table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hutchings's table is a 'working machine' for proof writing: for each statement type consult the 'Ways to Prove', 'Ways to Use', and 'How to Negate' columns. A proof is 'good' when each step matches an entry in this table—i.e., when every step is justifiable by the appropriate logical technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof (prove p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove p directly by deriving p from hypotheses; alternatively assume ¬p and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can prove p directly, do so; if assuming ¬p leads to a contradiction that shows p must hold, that is a valid alternative. In usage, once p is established it can be used as true; the negation is simply 'not p'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions (p and q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a conjunction by proving each component separately (prove p; prove q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a conjunction, you may use either component because both are true. The negation of (p and q) is (not p) or (not q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctions / proof by cases (p or q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a disjunction by proving one of the disjuncts (prove p or prove q), or to deduce a consequence r from a disjunction, show p⇒r and q⇒r (proof by cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can also assume ¬p and deduce q (or vice versa) to establish p∨q. The negation of (p or q) is (not p) and (not q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication: direct and contrapositive (p ⇒ q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove p⇒q by assuming p and deducing q (direct proof), or prove the contrapositive by assuming ¬q and deducing ¬p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either method is acceptable; remember the logical equivalence of an implication and its contrapositive. The negation of p⇒q is p and (not q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional / equivalence (p ⇔ q)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove p⇔q either by proving both implications (p⇒q and q⇒p) or by proving p∧q (if appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once established, p and q are interchangeable. The negation of p⇔q is (p ∧ ¬q) or (¬p ∧ q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs (∃x ∈ S P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove an existential statement by finding (constructing or exhibiting) an x in S with P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase such proofs as 'Let x ∈ S with P(x)'; the negation of an existential is a universal negation: ∀x∈S not P(x). Existence proofs often require an explicit example or a construction that yields the required witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal proofs (∀x ∈ S P(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a universal statement by letting x be an arbitrary element of S and showing P(x) holds (the arbitrary element method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'Let x be any element of S' and then prove P(x) without assuming special properties of x. The negation of a universal statement is the existence of a counterexample: ∃x∈S not P(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how to negate common statement types
rubrics_metrics.description: For each common logical form know the correct negation (useful for contradiction proofs and accurate reasoning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negations per the table: negation of p is not p; negation of p∧q is (not p) or (not q); negation of p∨q is (not p) and (not q); negation of p⇒q is p and (not q); negation of p⇔q is (p ∧ ¬q) or (¬p ∧ q); negation of ∃x P(x) is ∀x not P(x); negation of ∀x P(x) is ∃x not P(x). Use these patterns when designing proofs by contradiction or when translating informal negations into correct logical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each proof step justifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of good math writing is that each step of a proof matches a recognized logical move (as in the table) and is therefore justifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a proof, identify the logical form of the step and explicitly or implicitly invoke the appropriate rule or technique (e.g., 'by contrapositive', 'by case analysis', 'let x be arbitrary', 'take x = ...'). This makes the argument persuasive and clear to a reader trained in the same logical vocabulary.
